lead: Deutsch and Deutsch-Jozsa answer a yes/no question about a hidden Boolean function with one oracle call. The function is promised to be either constant or balanced. Classically, a deterministic check may need many inputs. The quantum circuit uses Hadamards to create a uniform superposition, calls the oracle once, and uses a second Hadamard layer. Phase kickback turns the function values into relative signs. Interference then sends a constant function to the all-zero output and a balanced function away from it. This is the smallest working example of the sign-to-bit trick used in later quantum algorithms.
prereq: You need: phase kickback from 4.1 and the Hadamard and controlled gates from Unit 3.

sections.h3: Deutsch's problem and the one-qubit circuit

blocks.text: The Deutsch problem gives one black-box function f:{0,1}→{0,1}. The promise says f is either constant, so f(0)=f(1), or balanced, so f(0)≠f(1). The task is to decide which with one oracle query. The oracle is a unitary U_f that maps |x⟩|y⟩ to |x⟩|y⊕f(x)⟩; x and y are one-bit labels and ⊕ is XOR.

items: Prepare |0⟩|1⟩: first qubit as input, second as ancilla.
Apply H to both qubits. The input becomes (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and the ancilla becomes (|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2.
Apply U_f once. The ancilla state stays |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 and the input picks up the sign (−1)^f(x).
Apply H to the first qubit only.
Measure the first qubit: 0 means constant, 1 means balanced.

blocks.where: a₀ is the amplitude for measuring the first qubit as 0; f(x) is the promised Boolean function; (−1)^f(x) is +1 when f(x)=0 and −1 when f(x)=1.

blocks.text: The Deutsch-Jozsa problem extends the promise to f:{0,1}^n→{0,1}. Balanced now means f(x)=1 on exactly half of the 2^n inputs, and constant means f(x) is the same for all inputs. The circuit uses n input qubits and one ancilla.

items: Apply H^⊗n to the input register and H to the ancilla; H^⊗n means H on each of the n input qubits.
Apply H^⊗n again to the input register.
Measure the input register in the standard basis.

blocks.where: a_{0^n} is the amplitude for measuring all n input qubits as 0; x runs over all 2^n bit strings; f(x) is the promised function; the probability of the all-zero outcome is |a_{0^n}|².

sections.h3: Why the promise and the second Hadamard matter

blocks.text: For a constant function, every term (−1)^f(x) has the same sign. The sum in the amplitude is ±2^n, so a_{0^n}=±1 and the all-zero probability is 1. For a balanced function, exactly 2^{n−1} terms are +1 and 2^{n−1} terms are −1. The sum is 0, so a_{0^n}=0 and the all-zero probability is 0.

The final H^⊗n is essential. Before it, the function values sit as relative signs between branches. A direct measurement would sample a uniformly random x and reveal almost nothing about constant versus balanced. The final Hadamards make the branches interfere. Constructive interference goes to the all-zero outcome only for a constant function; destructive interference removes it for a balanced function.

The promise is also essential. Without it, the same circuit still produces a probability distribution, but the all-zero outcome is not forced to be 1 or 0. A function that is neither constant nor balanced can give an intermediate amplitude, so one query cannot decide the property with certainty. Deutsch-Jozsa is a promise problem, not a general function classifier.

figure.caption: The input register starts in |0^n⟩ and the ancilla in |1⟩. After the oracle and the final Hadamards, measurement gives all zeros exactly when the promised function is constant.

spec.title: Deutsch-Jozsa circuit
spec.aria: A left-to-right circuit shows the input register passing through Hadamards, the oracle with an ancilla in |1⟩, a second Hadamard layer, and measurement.

examples.question: A two-qubit Deutsch-Jozsa test uses the promised function f(00)=0, f(01)=1, f(10)=1, f(11)=0. After the final Hadamards, what is the probability of measuring 00? Is f constant or balanced?
steps: List the four inputs and values: f(00)=0, f(01)=1, f(10)=1, f(11)=0. The target outcome is 00 on the two input qubits.
The amplitude for outcome 00 is a₀₀ = (1/2²) Σ_x (−1)^f(x). Here 2²=4 inputs and x runs over 00,01,10,11.
Divide by 4: a₀₀=0/4=0. The probability is |a₀₀|²=0²=0.0.
The all-zero outcome has probability 0.0, so it never occurs. Under the promise, f is balanced. It has two ones among four inputs.
examples.answer: The probability of measuring 00 is 0.0; f is balanced.

traps: Leaving out the final Hadamard layer. The signs are not visible to a standard measurement until interference converts them into an output bit.
Mixing the one-qubit Deutsch circuit with the n-qubit Deutsch-Jozsa circuit. Deutsch uses one input qubit; Deutsch-Jozsa uses n input qubits and H^⊗n.
Ignoring the promise. Deutsch-Jozsa decides constant versus balanced only under the promise; it is not a general classifier of arbitrary Boolean functions.
Using f(x) instead of (−1)^f(x) in the amplitude sum. The oracle writes a sign, so the term is +1 for f(x)=0 and −1 for f(x)=1.
Preparing the ancilla in |0⟩. The standard circuit starts the ancilla in |1⟩ so that H makes |−⟩ and phase kickback works.

quiz.q: In the one-qubit Deutsch circuit, what is the initial two-qubit state and what does a measurement result of 1 mean?
quiz.a: Start in |0⟩|1⟩. Result 1 means f is balanced.

quiz.q: Why does the ancilla start in |1⟩ and then receive a Hadamard?
quiz.a: The Hadamard makes |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2. The oracle then writes (−1)^f(x) into the sign by phase kickback.

quiz.q: For f(0)=0 and f(1)=1 in Deutsch's algorithm, what is the measurement result with certainty?
quiz.a: f is balanced. The amplitude for 0 is (1/2)(1−1)=0, so the result is 1 with probability 1.

quiz.q: In the worked example f(00)=0, f(01)=1, f(10)=1, f(11)=0, what is P(00)?
Why is the Deutsch-Jozsa promise needed for a deterministic one-query answer?
quiz.a: Without the promise, the all-zero amplitude can be neither ±1 nor 0. A function that is neither constant nor balanced can give an intermediate probability, so one query cannot decide the property with certainty.

quiz.q: In Deutsch-Jozsa, what outcome is certain for a constant function?
What goes wrong if the final H^⊗n layer is left out?
quiz.a: The relative signs remain unmeasured. A measurement samples x uniformly from the superposition and does not read constant versus balanced.

quiz.q: How does n=1 Deutsch relate to Deutsch-Jozsa?
quiz.a: Deutsch is Deutsch-Jozsa with one input qubit. The same H-U_f-H-measure pattern applies.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Deutsch-Jozsa problem is mainly a proof that a quantum computer can beat any deterministic classical algorithm in query complexity for a promise problem. Later algorithms replace the single oracle with structured unitaries and repeated interference. Search terms: exact quantum query complexity, promise problems, and phase kickback in the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm.
